# Human-Machine Governance and the Data Flywheel\chaptersubtitle{Bumpless Override, Intervention Tagging, and Telemetry Lineage}

![**Systems Organ Focus: Stage 7 (Human Authority, Bumpless Override & Governed Lineage).** The governance subsystem arbitrates physical authority between human operators and learned policies, enforcing smooth bumpless transitions, preventing policy collapse through truncated episode slicing, and establishing cryptographic telemetry audit trails.](figures/fig_pipeline_locator.svg){#fig-locator-ch10 width=100% fig-pos="H"}

*Why does retraining a robot on logs of human emergency interventions cause it to drive straight into walls?*

In digital software platforms, user interaction logs are routinely ingested into training pipelines to improve recommendation models through passive data flywheels. In Physical AI, an embodied agent actively shapes its own future data distribution. When human operators seize physical controls to prevent an imminent collision, unmanaged telemetry engines record both the dangerous drift and the human correction as an unbroken demonstration, causing behavioral cloning models to learn fatal spurious correlations. Governance in Physical AI is not an administrative afterthought; it is an active systems contract that arbitrates real-time authority between human supervisors and learned policies via $\mathcal{C}^2$ bumpless transfer, prevents policy collapse through microsecond intervention demarcation, and secures cryptographic audit trails for physical operations.

{{< pagebreak >}}

::: {.callout-objective}
By the conclusion of this chapter, you will be able to:

1. **Design Human-Machine Authority State Machines:** Implement deterministic authority transitions (Manual $\leftrightarrow$ Shared $\leftrightarrow$ Autonomous $\leftrightarrow$ E-Stop) with strict hardware preemption guarantees.
2. **Formulate and Implement Bumpless Transfer Filters:** Eliminate motor torque spikes, high-frequency jerk ($\dddot{q}$), and gearbox shock during sudden human joystick takeovers using $\mathcal{C}^2$ smoothstep blending.
3. **Mitigate Policy Endogeneity and Covariate Shift:** Apply microsecond intervention tagging and truncated episode slicing to prevent behavioral cloning policy collapse during continuous data flywheel retraining.
4. **Establish Tamper-Evident Telemetry and Cryptographic Lineage:** Implement IEEE 1588 PTP hardware timestamping and SHA-256 hash chains binding sensory observations, model weights, and physical actuator actions.
5. **Freeze the Human-Authority and Governance Record (authority design):** Construct the tenth milestone artifact of the engineering notebook establishing authority contracts, blending bounds, and automated dual-bank firmware rollback protocols.
:::

## The Illusion of Pure Autonomy

In digital machine learning, an autonomous agent operates in a closed virtual sandbox: if an algorithm makes an erroneous prediction, the runtime engine logs a warning, resets the environment seed, or yields a negative reward penalty. In the physical world, an un-governed motor command shears stainless-steel transmission gears, tears timing belts, or strikes a human collaborator. 

No embodied AI system is ever truly isolated from human governance. Whether through direct teleoperation, cooperative shared admittance, dead-man consent heartbeats, or emergency-stop interlocks, human authority remains the foundational safety layer of physical engineering. However, introducing human intervention into an embodied AI architecture creates two severe systems challenges:

1. **The Mechanical Transition Shock:** When a human operator abruptly deflects an analog joystick to override an erratic neural policy, the instantaneous step change in commanded torque $\Delta \mathbf{u}$ drives an impulse in torque rate-of-change ($\dot{\mathbf{u}} \to \infty$). In physical motor drives, this infinite jerk induces massive stator current inrushes ($I(t) \propto \tau(t)$), tripping inverter overcurrent fuses and driving gear tooth backlash collisions that rapidly destroy mechanical gearboxes.
2. **The Policy Endogeneity Trap:** In closed-loop physical systems, an agent's actions directly alter its environment ($W_t \xrightarrow{A_t} W_{t+1} \to O_{t+1}$), shaping its future observation distribution. When a human intervenes to avert an accident, logging the continuous trajectory without intervention tags poisons the training dataset. The retrained policy fits the pre-crash drift to the human's emergency recovery turn, learning that reckless driving is the prerequisite for correct operation.

Governing physical AI requires a dual-brain architecture: a deterministic, bare-metal microcontroller enforcing hard authority state machines and bumpless blending filters in real time, coupled with an audited data pipeline that enforces cryptographic lineage and truncated episode slicing.

::: {.callout-note icon=false}
* **CS / ML Systems Perspective:** Think of bumpless transfer as a real-time S-curve learning rate scheduler for physical torque, preventing discontinuity between human and model outputs.
* **EE / Robotics Perspective:** Bumpless transfer is an active tracking filter with integrator state synchronization that eliminates actuator jerk and inverter tripping during controller handoffs.
:::


## Human Authority and the Authority State Machine

Physical authority cannot be treated as an arbitrary boolean variable inside an untrusted application thread. If an operator pulls a manual emergency stop, that command must not wait in a Linux inter-process communication (IPC) message queue behind a blocked Vision-Language Model inference call.

Authority in Physical AI follows a strict, deterministic hierarchy implemented directly in bare-metal microcontroller silicon:

$$\begin{aligned}
\text{Priority 0 (E-Stop)} &> \text{Priority 1 (Manual Joystick)} \\
&> \text{Priority 2 (MCU Enforcer)} > \text{Priority 3 (MPU Policy)}
\end{aligned}$$

![**Deterministic Human--Machine Authority State Machine.** Operational authority transitions smoothly between Manual Override, Shared Control, and Autonomous Lease modes. Physical human inputs and zero-software hardware interlocks maintain absolute preemption privileges over learned neural proposals.](figures/fig10_authority_state_machine.svg){#fig-authority-state-machine width=100%}

### The Four Operational Authority States

As illustrated in @fig-authority-state-machine, the runtime environment transitions between four discrete operational states:

1. **Manual Override (Direct Teleoperation):** The human operator exercises primary authority over the machine via an analog joystick, teach pendant, or haptic master arm. The neural policy proposal stream on the Linux MPU is disabled or relegated to a passive observer. The real-time microcontroller (MCU) continues to enforce kinematic joint limits and velocity clamps, while simultaneously running an active tracking observer to synchronize internal controller states.
2. **Shared / Cooperative Control:** Actuator control is dynamically blended between human intent and learned foundation policies. The operator provides high-level guidance or impedance bias, while the neural policy assists with trajectory stabilization, obstacle avoidance, or fine precision insertion. Blended commands are arbitrated via dynamic admittance:
 $$\mathbf{u}(t) = \alpha(t) \mathbf{u}_{\text{human}}(t) + (1 - \alpha(t)) \mathbf{u}_{\text{policy}}(t)$$

3. **Autonomous Lease:** The neural policy proposes multi-step action chunk splines at $20\,\text{Hz}$ from the Linux MPU. The real-time MCU validates each proposal against $1000\,\text{Hz}$ Control Barrier Functions ($h(x) \ge 0$) and dynamic stopping distances ($d_{\text{stop}}$). Autonomy is gated by an active **Dead-Man Consent Lease**: the operator must continuously assert a physical presence heartbeat (e.g. capacitive grip sensor, foot pedal, or optical presence curtain) refreshed every $t_{\text{lease}} \le 200\,\text{ms}$. If the lease expires, authority immediately reverts.
4. **Category 0 / 1 Emergency Stop (Zero-Software Interlock):** The ultimate physical fail-safe state. Depressing a physical emergency stop button or tripping the hardware watchdog drops safety-rated contactor relays, physically disconnecting motor power buses and engaging mechanical spring-applied friction brakes.

| Authority State | Primary Authority | Substrate | Entry Condition / Trigger | Active Invariants & Enforcements |
| :--- | :--- | :--- | :--- | :--- |
| **1. Manual Override** | Human Operator | MCU Bare-Metal / SPI | Operator seizes control ($\|\mathbf{u}_{\text{h}}\| > \delta_{\text{takeover}}$) | Clamps joint limits ($q \in [q_{\text{min}}, q_{\text{max}}]$); runs integrator tracking sync. |
| **2. Shared Control** | Human + Policy | MCU Blending Filter | Cooperative task engagement | $\mathcal{C}^2$ quintic blending; bounds torque derivative $\|\dot{\mathbf{u}}\| \le a_{\text{max}}$. |
| **3. Autonomous Lease** | Neural MPU Policy | Linux MPU + Edge NPU | Consent heartbeat active ($t_{\text{lease}} < 200\,\text{ms}$) | 1000 Hz CBF enforcers ($h(x) \ge 0$); dynamic stopping check $d_{\text{gap}} > d_{\text{stop}}$. |
| **4. Hardware E-Stop** | Hardware Interlock | Dedicated Safety Relay | Physical button pressed, watchdog trip | Zero-software contactor disconnect; spring friction brakes locked. |

### Preemption Privileges and Consent Heartbeats

To ensure an operator can seize control at any moment without fighting an active neural policy, the MCU continuously monitors raw analog joystick deflection. When the operator applies a command exceeding the deadband threshold:

$$\|\mathbf{u}_{\text{human}}(t)\| > \delta_{\text{takeover}}$$

the MCU's real-time timer interrupt instantly triggers a **Preemptive Takeover Event**. The autonomous proposal pipeline is stripped of authority within $< 1\,\text{ms}$, and the control loop activates the bumpless blending filter to transition smoothly to manual control.

::: {.callout-note title="Cross-Embodiment Anchor: Human Authority and Governed Lineage Across the 3 Archetypes"}
* **Archetype 1: Locomotion & Mobility (Autonomous Vehicles & Delivery Drones):** 
 In an autonomous delivery van, the safety driver touches the steering wheel with torque $> 2\text{ N}\cdot\text{m}$. The chassis MCU instantly triggers a Preemptive Takeover Event, executing a $100\text{ ms}$ $\mathcal{C}^2$ smoothstep torque blend that transfers steering authority without jerking the wheels off the lane. The event triggers truncated episode slicing, tagging the intervention in telemetry logs to prevent policy endogeneity collapse.

* **Archetype 2: Contact Manipulation (The Desk Bench Kit / Manipulator):** 
 In cooperative assembly, an operator grasps the teach pendant to adjust a misaligned insertion trajectory. The Cortex-M4 MCU detects deadband displacement ($\|\mathbf{u}_{\text{human}}\| > 0.05\text{ rad}$), blends control authority via quintic smoothstep polynomials ($\tau_{\text{blend}} = 80\text{ ms}$), and clamps motor torque rates ($\|\dot{\mathbf{u}}\| \le 11\text{ N}\cdot\text{m/s}$), preventing inverter overcurrent tripping and gear tooth shock.

* **Archetype 3: Cybernetic Energy (Smart Grid Substation Dispatch):** 
 A utility transmission operator issues an emergency manual re-dispatch command during a severe storm. The substation grid supervisor initiates a $200\text{ ms}$ ramp rate limiter on battery storage inverters, smoothly overriding autonomous reinforcement learning dispatch setpoints without exciting subsynchronous grid resonance or inducing frequency transients on the 50/60 Hz bus.
:::


## Bumpless Control Overrides and Jerk-Bounded Blending


In theoretical control software, switching between two controllers is modeled as a discrete multiplexer switch:

$$\mathbf{u}(t) = \begin{cases} \mathbf{u}_{\text{policy}}(t), & t < t_{\text{takeover}} \\ \mathbf{u}_{\text{human}}(t), & t \ge t_{\text{takeover}} \end{cases}$$

In physical hardware, this step transition is catastrophic. 

### The Physics of Mechanical Torque Shock

Consider an articulated manipulator where Joint 2 is commanded by a neural policy to hold position against gravity with $\mathbf{u}_{\text{policy}} = 0.4\,\text{Nm}$. At $t = 100\,\text{ms}$, an operator abruptly pulls the teleoperation joystick to command an evasive velocity requiring $\mathbf{u}_{\text{human}} = 1.1\,\text{Nm}$. 

If the controller switches instantaneously, the step error $\Delta \mathbf{u} = +0.7\,\text{Nm}$ produces a theoretical impulse in torque derivative:

$$\dot{\mathbf{u}}(t) = \frac{d\mathbf{u}}{dt} \longrightarrow \infty$$

Because electromagnetic torque in brushless DC (BLDC) motors is proportional to stator quadrature current ($\tau = K_t I_q$), the Field-Oriented Control (FOC) inverter attempts to deliver an instantaneous current spike. As shown in @fig-bumpless-transfer(c), this current surge spikes past the driver's overcurrent trip threshold ($I_{\text{trip}} = 6.0\,\text{A}$), tripping hardware fault protection and shutting down the motor driver. 

Simultaneously, the sudden torque step excites high-frequency mechanical resonances, slamming gear teeth across backlash gaps, accelerating gear tooth pitting, and causing audible mechanical shudder.

![**Comparison of Hard Step Takeover vs. $\mathcal{C}^2$ Bumpless Torque Blending.** (a) Commanded control torque $u(t)$ during a $0.7\,\text{Nm}$ human takeover at $t = 100\,\text{ms}$. (b) Torque rate-of-change $\dot{u}(t) \propto \dddot{q}(t)$ reveals a severe Dirac impulse during hard switching versus a bounded, smooth bell curve ($\le 11\,\text{Nm/s}$) under bumpless blending. (c) Motor phase current $I(t)$ demonstrates how hard switching induces a $7.4\,\text{A}$ inrush spike that trips overcurrent limits, whereas bumpless blending maintains safe, continuous current delivery.](figures/fig10_bumpless_transfer.svg){#fig-bumpless-transfer width=100%}

### The $\mathcal{C}^2$ Smoothstep Blending Formulation

To eliminate torque steps and bound mechanical jerk, the MCU routes all authority transitions through a **Bumpless Blending Filter**. Rather than switching instantaneously, the active control law blends the sources across a configurable time window $\tau_{\text{blend}} \in [50, 150]\,\text{ms}$:

$$\mathbf{u}_{\text{actuator}}(t) = (1 - \alpha(\sigma)) \mathbf{u}_{\text{policy}}(t) + \alpha(\sigma) \mathbf{u}_{\text{human}}(t)$$

where $\sigma$ is the normalized transition progress:

$$\sigma(t) = \frac{t - t_{\text{takeover}}}{\tau_{\text{blend}}}, \quad \sigma \in [0, 1]$$

To guarantee that the first derivative (acceleration) and second derivative (jerk) remain strictly continuous ($\mathcal{C}^2$ continuity) at the boundaries $\sigma = 0$ and $\sigma = 1$, we employ a **quintic smoothstep polynomial**:

$$\alpha(\sigma) = 6\sigma^5 - 15\sigma^4 + 10\sigma^3$$

Differentiating with respect to time yields the smooth transition derivatives:

$$\dot{\alpha}(\sigma) = \frac{1}{\tau_{\text{blend}}} \left( 30\sigma^4 - 60\sigma^3 + 30\sigma^2 \right)$$

$$\ddot{\alpha}(\sigma) = \frac{1}{\tau_{\text{blend}}^2} \left( 120\sigma^3 - 180\sigma^2 + 60\sigma \right)$$

Evaluating at the endpoints confirms complete derivative containment:

$$\dot{\alpha}(0) = \dot{\alpha}(1) = 0, \quad \ddot{\alpha}(0) = \ddot{\alpha}(1) = 0$$

Under this formulation, the maximum torque derivative during a step input $\Delta \mathbf{u}$ is bounded deterministically:

$$\|\dot{\mathbf{u}}(t)\|_{\text{max}} \le \frac{1.875}{\tau_{\text{blend}}} \|\Delta \mathbf{u}\| \le j_{\text{max}}$$

For $\Delta \mathbf{u} = 0.7\,\text{Nm}$ and $\tau_{\text{blend}} = 100\,\text{ms}$, the peak torque rate is strictly bounded at $13.1\,\text{Nm/s}$, safely below the mechanical gearhead limit ($j_{\text{max}} = 15.0\,\text{Nm/s}$) and preventing overcurrent trips.

| Parameter | Mathematical Constraint | Real-Time Substrate | Physical Function on Mechanism |
| :--- | :--- | :--- | :--- |
| **Blending Window ($\tau_{\text{blend}}$)** | $\tau_{\text{blend}} \in [50, 150]\,\text{ms}$ | MCU 1000 Hz ISR | Establishes finite transition time between policy proposal and human control. |
| **Polynomial Order** | $\alpha(\sigma) = 6\sigma^5 - 15\sigma^4 + 10\sigma^3$ | Static Floating-Point | Guarantees $\mathcal{C}^2$ continuity ($\dot{\alpha} = \ddot{\alpha} = 0$ at boundaries). |
| **Acceleration Bound ($a_{\text{max}}$)** | $\|\dot{\mathbf{u}}(t)\| \le a_{\text{max}}$ | Hardware Current Loop | Eliminates stator coil inrush current spikes ($I(t) \le I_{\text{continuous}}$). |
| **Jerk Bound ($j_{\text{max}}$)** | $\|\ddot{\mathbf{u}}(t)\| \le j_{\text{max}}$ | MCU Safety Enforcer | Eliminates gearbox tooth backlash shock and torsional resonance vibration. |
| **Tracking Integrator Sync** | $\dot{x}_{\text{int}} = \frac{1}{\tau_{\text{track}}}(x_{\text{actual}} - x_{\text{int}})$ | Real-Time Loop State | Prevents PID integrator windup bump when human control loop takes over. |
: Bumpless Transfer and Blending Filter Parameters. Every parameter maps directly to hardware timing and mechanical protection constraints. {#tbl-bumpless-parameters}

### Integrator Windup and Controller State Synchronization

A subtle failure mode in human takeover occurs when the human's manual controller (e.g. an impedance or PID loop on the host workstation) runs in the background while the robot is under autonomous control. 

If the robot's physical position deviates slightly from the human's joystick setpoint during autonomous execution, the human controller's internal integral term ($\int e(t) dt$) accumulates a massive error charge—a phenomenon known as **integrator windup**. When authority transfers, this charged integrator discharges into the motors, causing a violent instantaneous jerk even if the feedforward joystick command is centered.

To prevent integrator windup bumps, the human control loop must execute **Active State Synchronization** during autonomous mode:

$$\dot{x}_{\text{human\_int}}(t) = \frac{1}{\tau_{\text{track}}} \left( x_{\text{actual}}(t) - x_{\text{human\_int}}(t) \right)$$

By continuously slaving the inactive controller's internal state to the actual physical plant, the integrator error is identically zero at the instant of takeover ($t = t_{\text{takeover}}$), ensuring a clean, shudder-free handoff.


## Policy Endogeneity and the Governed Data Flywheel

Modern embodied AI architectures rely on continuous learning: robots collect interaction telemetry in the field, upload rollouts to the cloud, fine-tune behavioral cloning (BC) or diffusion policies, and deploy updated model weights over-the-air (OTA). 

This feedback cycle is commonly known as the **Data Flywheel**. However, in physical systems, an un-governed data flywheel creates an insidious failure mode: **Policy Endogeneity**.

![**Policy Endogeneity: Naive Flywheel vs. Governed Episode Slicing.** In a naive data flywheel (top), un-tagged human intervention logs contaminate training datasets with spurious causal correlations, causing catastrophic policy collapse. Under governed episode slicing (bottom), the MCU tags the exact takeover timestamp, discards pre-crash failure buffers, and isolates human recovery demonstrations with cryptographic SHA-256 lineage.](figures/fig10_policy_endogeneity_flywheel.svg){#fig-policy-endogeneity width=100%}

### The Intervention Poisoning Paradox

In classical imitation learning, training data is assumed to be sampled from an expert stationary distribution (@ross2011reduction). On a physical robot deployed in the field, this assumption is fundamentally violated whenever a human operator intervenes to prevent an accident.

Consider the causal sequence during an intervention event:

1. **The Drift Phase ($t \in [t_{\text{takeover}} - T_{\text{discard}}, t_{\text{takeover}}]$):** The autonomous policy drifts out of distribution due to optical glare, mechanical backlash, or unexpected obstacle placement. The robot accelerates directly toward a structural warehouse pillar.
2. **The Takeover Event ($t = t_{\text{takeover}}$):** The human operator panics, grabs the joystick, and applies maximum counter-steering torque.
3. **The Recovery Phase ($t \in [t_{\text{takeover}}, t_{\text{takeover}} + T_{\text{recover}}]$):** The human maneuvers the robot safely around the pillar back to the nominal path.

If the logging pipeline records this continuous episode naively and appends it to the training dataset $\mathcal{D}_{\text{train}}$, empirical risk minimization fits model parameters $\theta$ across the entire stream:

$$\min_\theta \sum_{t} \mathcal{L}\left( \pi_\theta(O_t), a_t \right)$$

Because the high-speed approach toward the pillar ($O_{t-k}$) is immediately followed by a sharp right turn ($a_t = \text{steer\_right}$), the neural network learns a poisonous spurious correlation:

$$P\left(a_t = \text{steer\_right} \mid \text{DistanceToPillar} < 0.3\,\text{m}, v > 1.5\,\text{m/s}\right) \approx 1.0$$

When the retrained policy is deployed back to the fleet, it does not avoid pillars; it deliberately drives straight toward structural pillars at high velocity, waiting until the final fraction of a second to attempt an emergency turn. Because physical inertia ($m \mathbf{v}$) and stopping distance constraints cannot be overcome at speed, the retrained fleet systematically collides with warehouse infrastructure—a total **Policy Collapse**.

### The Truncated Episode Slicing Protocol

To transform field interventions from dataset poison into safe, high-value training signals, the governance engine implements **Truncated Episode Slicing**:

| Trajectory Phase | Time Boundary | Hardware & Logging Action | Destination Partition |
| :--- | :--- | :--- | :--- |
| **Nominal Execution** | $[0, t_{\text{takeover}} - T_{\text{discard}}]$ | Clean autonomous tracking | Nominal Behavioral Cloning ($\mathcal{D}_{\text{nominal}}$) |
| **Pre-Crash Drift** | $[t_{\text{takeover}} - T_{\text{discard}}, t_{\text{takeover}}]$ | Discarded from training; flagged as pre-failure | Negative Failure Buffer ($\mathcal{D}_{\text{fail}}$) |
| **Human Recovery** | $[t_{\text{takeover}}, t_{\text{recover}}]$ | Tagged with hardware PTP timestamp | Recovery Adaptation Dataset ($\mathcal{D}_{\text{recover}}$) |

1. **Microsecond Intervention Tagging:** The instant $\|\mathbf{u}_{\text{human}}\| > \delta_{\text{takeover}}$, the real-time MCU stamps the telemetry packet with an immutable hardware PTP timestamp $t_{\text{takeover}}$ and flags the stream as `INTERVENTION_ACTIVE`.
2. **Pre-Takeover Slicing ($T_{\text{discard}}$):** The ingestion pipeline automatically discards the preceding $T_{\text{discard}} = 2.0\,\text{seconds}$ of autonomous trajectory prior to takeover. This pre-crash drift is routed to a dedicated **Negative Failure Buffer** ($\mathcal{D}_{\text{fail}}$) used exclusively for counterfactual safety verification and out-of-distribution detection.
3. **Recovery Demonstration Partitioning:** The human recovery trajectory $[t_{\text{takeover}}, t_{\text{recover}}]$ is isolated and assigned to a **Recovery Adaptation Dataset** ($\mathcal{D}_{\text{recover}}$). In this dataset, samples are explicitly conditioned on a recovery intent token or used in goal-conditioned DAgger formulations (@ross2011reduction).
4. **Nominal Slice Retention:** Only the validated, non-intervened trajectory $[0, t_{\text{takeover}} - T_{\text{discard}}]$ enters the pristine nominal behavioral cloning dataset ($\mathcal{D}_{\text{nominal}}$).

| Slicing Regime | Time Window Relative to Takeover | Destination Dataset | Purpose & Model Training Impact |
| :--- | :--- | :--- | :--- |
| **Nominal Slice** | $[0, t_{\text{takeover}} - T_{\text{discard}}]$ | $\mathcal{D}_{\text{nominal}}$ (Pristine) | Standard behavioral cloning; free from drift and human panic artifacts. |
| **Pre-Crash Drift** | $[t_{\text{takeover}} - T_{\text{discard}}, t_{\text{takeover}}]$ | $\mathcal{D}_{\text{fail}}$ (Negative Buffer) | Discarded from BC; used for offline hazard analysis and OOD detection. |
| **Human Recovery** | $[t_{\text{takeover}}, t_{\text{recover}}]$ | $\mathcal{D}_{\text{recover}}$ (Corrective) | Conditioned recovery policy training; teaches stabilization from boundary states. |
: The Truncated Episode Slicing Protocol. Strict dataset partitioning prevents intervention-induced covariate shift while capturing valuable recovery demonstrations. {#tbl-slicing-rules}


## Microsecond PTP Logging and Cryptographic Lineage

For safety qualification, regulatory compliance, and post-incident autopsies, every physical action must be defensibly traceable to its originating sensory inputs, neural model weights, and software release version.

### IEEE 1588 Precision Time Protocol (PTP)

Physical AI systems operate across heterogeneous clock domains: image sensors capture photons at $60\,\text{Hz}$, the Linux MPU runs diffusion planning at $20\,\text{Hz}$, the real-time MCU executes safety enforcers at $1000\,\text{Hz}$, and motor inverters switch PWM at $20\,\text{kHz}$.

To ensure telemetry alignment, all compute nodes synchronize over Ethernet using **IEEE 1588v2 Precision Time Protocol (PTP)** hardware timestamping. Hardware MAC layers stamp packets at the physical transceiver boundary, achieving sub-microsecond synchronization ($\pm 1\,\mu\text{s}$) across the entire machine.

### Cryptographic Telemetry Lineage Chains

Every logged flight recorder packet carries a cryptographic hash chain binding its sensory observation $O_t$, proposed action $p_t$, MCU permitted action $u_t$, and active model weights:

$$\text{PacketHash}_t = \text{SHA-256}\left( \text{PacketHash}_{t-1} \,\|\, t_{\text{ptp}} \,\|\, O_t \,\|\, p_t \,\|\, u_t \,\|\, \text{ModelHash} \right)$$

This tamper-evident Merkle chain guarantees that after a physical incident, investigators can prove with mathematical certainty whether a motor torque was commanded by a specific neural network checkpoint, modified by the MCU safety barrier, or overridden by a human operator.

| Field Name | Data Type / Representation | Substrate & Source | Verification Function in Post-Incident Audit |
| :--- | :--- | :--- | :--- |
| `ptp_timestamp_ns` | `uint64_t` (Nanoseconds UTC) | IEEE 1588 Hardware MAC | Aligns multi-node sensor frames, IPC messages, and inverter currents. |
| `authority_state` | `enum {MANUAL, SHARED, AUTON, ESTOP}` | MCU State Register | Identifies which entity held primary physical authority during the millisecond. |
| `blend_alpha` | `float32` ($\alpha \in [0.0, 1.0]$) | MCU Blending Filter | Records exact weighting between human joystick and neural proposal. |
| `model_weights_sha256` | `char[64]` (SHA-256 Digest) | MPU Secure Enclave | Binds physical telemetry to the exact versioned neural network artifact. |
| `dataset_lineage_sha256`| `char[64]` (SHA-256 Digest) | Cloud Training Ledger | Links model weights directly to audited training data partitions ($\mathcal{D}_{\text{clean}}$). |
| `telemetry_chain_hash` | `char[64]` (SHA-256 Merkle Node) | Flight Recorder Engine | Provides tamper-evident proof that log frames were not altered post-crash. |
: Cryptographic Telemetry Lineage Schema. Structured audit records guarantee end-to-end provenance from dataset curation to physical actuation. {#tbl-provenance-schema}


## Shadow Mode Evaluation and Dual-Bank Firmware Rollback

Deploying updated neural network weights or control firmware to physical machines in the field carries severe physical risk. A newly trained policy may perform flawlessly on synthetic validation datasets yet harbor dangerous out-of-distribution failure modes under physical bench lighting.

To eliminate release risks, governance enforces two deployment protocols:

### 1. Field Shadow Mode Execution

Before a newly trained candidate policy $\pi_{\text{candidate}}$ is granted physical actuator authority, it is deployed in **Shadow Mode**:

* **Baseline Actuation:** The active baseline policy $\pi_{\text{baseline}}$ executes on the MPU and drives the physical actuators through the MCU safety filter.
* **Concurrent Shadow Ingestion:** The candidate policy $\pi_{\text{candidate}}$ executes concurrently on the secondary NPU cores, consuming the live camera and sensor streams ($O_t$) in real time.
* **Proposals Logged but Gated:** The candidate policy's proposals $p_t^{\text{cand}}$ are logged to the flight recorder but blocked from reaching the motor CAN bus.
* **Automated Promotion Thresholds:** An automated evaluator compares candidate proposals against baseline decisions and human intervention triggers over a 100-hour soak period. The candidate model is promoted to active authority only if its proposed trajectories violate zero control barrier envelopes ($h(x) \ge 0$) and exhibit lower predicted intervention rates than the baseline.

### 2. Dual-Bank A/B Flash Memory Rollback

When firmware or neural network weights are updated over-the-air (OTA):

* **Partitioned Storage Banks:** The microcontroller's internal flash memory is partitioned into two independent banks: **Bank A (Active)** and **Bank B (Staging)**.
* **Background Staging:** New firmware binaries and quantized tensor weights are written to Bank B while Bank A continues normal operation.
* **Bootloader Hardware Watchdog:** Upon reboot, the bootloader attempts execution from Bank B and arms a **Hardware Rollback Watchdog Timer** ($t_{\text{watchdog}} = 60\,\text{seconds}$).
* **Automatic Failover:** If the new firmware fails to initialize communication transceivers, misses a sensor timing deadline, or fails self-test health assertions within 60 seconds, the hardware watchdog trips and automatically reboots the processor back into the known-good Golden Bank A firmware.


## Systems Fallacies and Pitfalls

::: {.callout-warning}
### Common Engineering Fallacies

* **Fallacy 1:** *"More data always improves a physical AI policy, even if collected from human intervention recoveries."* 
 *Correction:* Un-tagged human interventions contaminate behavioral cloning datasets with severe covariate shift. The neural network treats pre-crash drift states as nominal conditions that should trigger emergency turns, teaching the policy to drive recklessly into obstacles.
* **Fallacy 2:** *"A software override switch running in Python on Linux provides adequate human safety authority."* 
 *Correction:* Python garbage collection pauses, Linux kernel thread preemption, and high-load memory bus saturation introduce multi-hundred-millisecond latency spikes. Human override inputs must be routed directly to bare-metal microcontroller hardware interrupts, completely bypassing the high-level operating system.
* **Fallacy 3:** *"Bumpless transfer is only a cosmetic feature for operator joystick comfort."* 
 *Correction:* Step handoffs in torque produce unbounded torque derivatives ($\dot{\mathbf{u}} \to \infty$). In physical BLDC actuators, this infinite jerk drives severe inrush current spikes that trip inverter overcurrent protections and mechanical shock that rapidly destroys precision gear teeth.
* **Fallacy 4:** *"Over-the-air firmware updates can flash memory directly without dual-bank rollback hardware."* 
 *Correction:* A corrupted OTA update on a deployed physical robot can brick CAN and Ethernet communication controllers, requiring destructive manual disassembly in the field. Dual-bank A/B memory with hardware watchdog auto-rollback is mandatory.
:::

### Hands-on Realization: Lab 10 — Bumpless Transfer and Governed Lineage

Connect an analog dual-axis joystick to the **Arduino UNO Q Dual-Brain Kit** (ARM Cortex-M4 MCU + Linux MPU). Configure the Linux MPU to stream high-rate autonomous trajectory proposals while the MCU executes the real-time authority state machine. 

1. **Simulate Sudden Human Takeovers:** Trigger hard joystick overrides during active trajectory tracking. Measure motor phase current and torque derivatives on an oscilloscope, observing how hard switching causes severe current spikes ($> 6\,\text{A}$) and audible gearbox backlash shudder.
2. **Implement $\mathcal{C}^2$ Smoothstep Blending:** Flash the MCU with the quintic bumpless blending filter ($\tau_{\text{blend}} = 100\,\text{ms}$). Prove on telemetry captures that actuator jerk is strictly bounded ($\le 13\,\text{Nm/s}$) and current spikes are completely eliminated.
3. **Audit Intervention Data Slicing:** Record field rollouts containing manual interventions. Compare naive behavioral cloning retraining against the truncated episode slicing protocol, demonstrating on the bench fixture how naive fine-tuning induces policy collapse while sliced lineage maintains stable autonomous performance (`labs/10-bumpless-governance`).
:::
